newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-SAMPRAS TRIUMPHS DESPITE PERSONAL TRAGEDY.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS TRIUMPHS DESPITE PERSONAL TRAGEDY.

text.p: For Pete Sampras, 1996 will always be remembered as the year his coach and close friend Tim Gullikson died of brain cancer.
But it is a measure of the maturity of the 25-year-old American that he has managed to stay at the top of men's tennis despite his personal tragedy, making history in the process.

Sampras begins his campaign at the ATP world championship on Wednesday against Andre Agassi knowing that he will remain at the top of the world rankings whatever happens at the season-ending tournament.

The current U.S. Open champion joins Jimmy Connors and John McEnroe as the only player to have finished at the top of the sport for four consecutive years. Sampras has held the prestigious position at the end of every season since 1993.

The number one spot has taken a great deal of pressure off the American as he prepares to take on the best eight players in the world at the Hanover championship, which used to be known as the Masters.

"It makes it a little bit more relaxed knowing that, whatever happens here, I've got the number one in the bag," he said. "It has been a difficult year after the death of Tim Gullikson and a bit up and down."
"Mentally I feel great. Ready to go. Ready to grind this week."
The championship is regarded as the most prestigious event outside of the four grand slams ; Wimbledon and the Australian, U.S. and French Opens.
Sampras has had a mixed year in the grand slams. Although he won the U.S. Open, he went out in the quarter-finals of Wimbledon, beaten by eventual Dutch winner Richard Krajicek.

One of his most impressive performances of the year came at the French Open which is played on clay, his least favourite surface. Sampras reached the semifinals where he was beaten by tournament winner Russian Yevgeny Kafelnikov.

It was his best performance in seven years at Roland Garros and even more remarkable since it came shortly after Gullikson's death. For weeks Sampras has asked journalists not to ask him anything about his close friend.

Sampras is one of the few players on the tour who can make tennis look easy. Few things seem to come more naturally to his body that racing to the front of the court and playing a crisp volley at the net.
Yet the American, one of the most composed players on the circuit, has never gripped the imagination of the public like the colourful stars of the past such as McEnroe and Connors.
Sampras knows that people have noticed that the controversial personalities have gone out of the game and the sport is suffering in his homeland because of it.
"You don't have quite the personalities of a McEnroe, Lendl, Connors and Borg and you have guys now just going out and playing -- not acting like those guys acted in some way.

"When you had McEnroe-Borg rivalry, it was the classic rivalry. You had one guy who was calm and cool and you had McEnroe who was kind of hostile. People who don't follow tennis will watch that match.
"You really don't have that today. At least in the States, it is difficult to sell."
